passage:
Yash was nineteen the night he finally asked it, in the small study circle after Sunday prayers: "What if I can't believe some of this?" A few people shifted in their seats. Shalini put down her cup and smiled. "That question is older than any of us in this room," she said. "Sit with it, and come back and tell me what you find." Nobody scolded him, and he left feeling curious more than afraid.

By the second year at college he had stopped going to the prayers in the hostel. He borrowed books from the library that he would have hidden from his grandmother, argued late into the night with Tenzin, who practised another faith, and with Rohan, who practised none. The old certainty loosened like a jar lid. It felt like freedom, and also like losing a room in the house he had grown up in.

In March he woke on a Sunday and felt nothing. No anger, no relief, just a quiet where the meaning had sat. He walked to the tea stall, sat with his cup, and did not pretend to have an answer. He wrote one line to Shalini: "Still asking." She answered the same evening: "Good. Keep asking honestly."

qa.q: Where did Yash first ask his question about belief?
qa.a: He asked in the small study circle after Sunday prayers.

qa.q: How did Shalini's answer differ from what Yash might have feared, and how did it matter later in March?
qa.a: She met his question with interest, said it was very old and common, and did not shame him, so when he felt empty in March he could still write to her honestly and get a welcome.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when he woke up on the Sunday in March?
qa.a: He felt hollow and quiet, with no anger or relief, and did not pretend to have an answer.

qa.q: How could Yash respond to the emptiness without rushing to a firm conclusion?
qa.a: He can keep asking honestly and stay in touch with people who welcome his questions, such as Shalini, instead of forcing an answer.

grounding: Three stages of a faith journey through doubt: an elder welcoming first questions, distance and loosened certainty away from home, and a quiet emptiness that is allowed to stay unresolved.
